Simple Past Tense of Be (Review of all forms)
The verb to be is used in different ways. When it is used in its past simple form it only has two forms, was and were .
Using standard components was Lowe's main argument to start with the new microcomputer's production.
The verb to be has different uses.
It helps us identify what the role of the subject was: Apple II was a successful microcomputer.
It is used to describe how something was (used with an adjective): The first computers were big and slow.
It is also used to talk about the location of something: IBM already was in New York during the 1960's.

How to Summarize a text?
When you need to summarize a text it is important that you understand it very well, so you can write only the most relevant facts and conclusions.
These are useful tips that help you to create a summarizing text.
1.  As we mention previously, you should read thoroughly the text, make sure you understand the main ideas and the general meaning.
2. Be careful with hidden information, sometimes you have to “read between lines”.
3. Highlight the main points of the text, important ideas you might want to include in the summarizing text. You can also use diagrams or pictures to help the understanding process.
Be careful!

Don't get confused. Remember that a summarizing is a short and easy text to read which contains the most relevant information. You should write the text in your own words, and do not use fragments from the original.
Remember that successful reading is easier when the text shows correct grammar, punctuation and coherence.

The IBM PC and the Rise of Microsoft

After the Apple II and other initial microcomputers were successful back in the late 70s, IBM®, the American multinational technology company, started to consider joining the market. By July 1980 Bill Lowe, chief of level systems division, made a presentation to IBM senior management on why the company had to make a move. Using standard components was Lowe's main argument to start with the new microcomputer's production. Management got an agree and the project received the green light. The device was ready in less than a year.

Its microprocessor was an Intel 8088. Both the operating system and a version of the BASIC programming language were supplied by Microsoft®; Tando provided the Disk drives; the printers came from Epson, and the Word processor and spreadsheet were among its applications software.</br></br>Was it successful? Yes, it was a commercial success. There was no microcomputer like it and by August 12th, 1981 IBM was forced to quadruple its production. Since the standard components for this microcomputer were provided by other outsourcing manufacturers, anybody was able to copy the design. IBM then decided to license the PC's operating system and looked for Microsoft's aid to do so.

How did they do it? Although Microsoft didn't have an operating system, Steve Jobs quickly bought one called QDOS from another small company. It was renamed MS-DOS and licensed to IBM. However, a contending company developed a rival operating system called DR-DOS. IBM's operating system was then renamed PC-DOS. Both the core of the battle and the economic success were in the development of operating systems. </br></br>In spite of making an alliance with IBM to develop DOS successor's called OS/2, Microsoft quit the project and focused on the development of something called Windows NT. In 1992 Windows 3.11 was released and was the first to successfully use a graphical user interface.
